explanations.answer: He wishes it were burning already
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says, "I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49). He isn't wishing for more time here. He's wishing it were already burning. I think that tells us how much this matters to Him.

explanations.answer: He wishes it could wait a while
explanations.explanation: I get it, friend. When I hear "fire," I want the oven timer reset too. But Jesus says the opposite: "…how I wish it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49). He isn't asking for more time, He wants it burning already.

explanations.answer: He wishes it would go out soon
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Jesus says He came to ignite this fire, and then adds, "…how I wish it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49). That's a wish for it to be burning, not for it to go out. Nothing in His words says He wants it put out.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says, "But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:50). So He isn't calm and settled. He says He is distressed until it is accomplished. I'd have to be honest and say that one sounds heavy.

Right, friend. Jesus doesn't say He's calm and settled. He says, "…how distressed I am until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:50). That word "distressed" is a big one. It's a good thing we read what He actually says, because calm and settled is nowhere in there.

You got it, baker. Jesus asks, "Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth?" and then answers: "No, I tell you, but division." (Luke 12:51). I think that one lands like a bakery with no cookies in it, because it's the opposite of what the crowd was expecting. Then He says households will be divided, five in one home, three against two and two against three (Luke 12:52). I think this is a heavy part, so let it sit a second.

I'd love that answer too, friend. Rest sounds wonderful after a long day at the bakery. But Jesus says, "No, I tell you, but division." (Luke 12:51). He says it right after saying He didn't come to bring peace. Rest isn't in the verse.

Healing is a good word, friend. But in this verse Jesus says, "Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division." (Luke 12:51). Division is the word He picks here. Healing doesn't show up.

That's right, friend. Jesus says they "…will be divided, father against son and son against father…" (Luke 12:53). He goes on to say mother against daughter and daughter against mother, too. He lists it out both ways. It's a tough list to hear.

I see why you'd hesitate, friend. It's a hard thing to hear. But Jesus says it plainly: "…father against son and son against father…" (Luke 12:53). He also names mothers and daughters, and mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law. So fathers and sons are right there on the list.

Right on the money, baker. Jesus says, "As soon as you see a cloud rising in the west, you say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and that is what happens." (Luke 12:54). They see the cloud and they call it. Then the rain shows up.

Brrr, friend, that's a chilly guess. But Jesus says the crowds see a cloud rising in the west and say, "A shower is coming…" (Luke 12:54). A shower is rain, not frost. And the text says that is what happens.

Wind is close, friend, since it shows up in the very next verse. There Jesus says that when the south wind blows, you say, "It will be hot…" (Luke 12:55). But for the cloud rising in the west, the crowds say, "A shower is coming…" (Luke 12:54). That one's rain.

That's the one, baker. Jesus says, "And when the south wind blows, you say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is." (Luke 12:55). Those crowds read the weather well. Two for two, and the weather agrees with them both times.

Close on the weather idea, friend, but this wind goes the other way. Jesus says, "…when the south wind blows, you say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is." (Luke 12:55). So the south wind means hot, not cold. Time to put the sweater back.

Good guess, friend, wind and storms feel like they go together. But Jesus says the crowds say, "It will be hot…" and then adds, "and it is." (Luke 12:55). Hot is what the south wind brings in this verse. Stormy isn't the word.

You nailed it, baker. Jesus says, "You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?" (Luke 12:56). They can read a cloud, but He asks why they can't read the present time. That's the point of His question.

Good thinking, friend, but scrolls aren't in this verse. Jesus asks, "Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?" (Luke 12:56). The crowds can read earth and sky just fine. The thing they're missing is the present time.

Dreams would be a fun thing to read, friend, but Jesus doesn't bring them up here. He says, "You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?" (Luke 12:56). The present time is the one He names.

Not quite, friend. Jesus asks the opposite: "And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right?" (Luke 12:57). He doesn't say to hand it off to someone else. He asks why they aren't judging for themselves.

Right, friend. Jesus asks, "And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right?" (Luke 12:57). He's pointing them to judge for themselves, not to let someone else decide. It's like me asking why you'd ask a neighbor if the dough looks right when the bowl is sitting in front of you.

That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate." (Luke 12:58). Notice He says "every effort." That's not a quick shrug and a "my bad," that's me hustling like my cookies are in the oven and the timer's already screaming. Do it on the road, while there's still road.

I know that road, friend. I've argued over a cookie or two myself. But Jesus says, "Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate." (Luke 12:58). Reconcile is the word, not argue.

Nice try, friend, but this isn't a bake-off. Jesus says, "Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate." (Luke 12:58). Reconcile is the word He uses. Competing doesn't get a mention.
Not quite, friend. Jesus says, "I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny." (Luke 12:59). So you don't get out early. You stay until the very last penny is paid.

Right, friend. Jesus says, "I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny." (Luke 12:59). So no early exit. That's the reason He says to reconcile while you're still on the way.
